name: Slack Pro
tagline: Run a small private team chat with channels, threads, files, and search

pricing.notes: Official Pro monthly seat price with annual billing; month-to-month is higher.

verdictSummary: A consolation build is possible, but the paid product's decisive value sits outside a solo rebuild. For Slack Pro, run a small private team chat with channels, threads, files, and search. The hard boundary is existing team network, integrations, push delivery, enterprise controls, and global reliability, plus network, moderation, and communication infrastructure.
coreLoopDIY: Run a small private team chat with channels, threads, file sharing, and search, and keep membership and moderation under the owner's control.
whatYouLose: existing team network, integrations, push delivery, enterprise controls, and global reliability
ongoingBurden: realtime delivery, notifications, abuse handling, search, media, permissions, mobile clients, backups, and community operations
whyPeopleStillPay: People still pay for Slack Pro because community software is valuable when members are already there and the operator does not have to own realtime reliability and abuse response. The recurring cost buys realtime delivery, notifications, abuse handling, search, media, permissions, mobile clients, backups, and community operations, not just the visible interface.

priorArt.name: Discourse
priorArt.desc: Mature open-source community discussion platform with strong moderation and search.

alternatives.name: Chanty Free
alternatives.desc: Five users get unlimited history, files, tasks and one-to-one calls; larger teams meet the paywall.

alternatives.name: Element
alternatives.desc: Rooms, threads, files and encrypted calls on Matrix; the free public service avoids server duty.

alternatives.name: Mattermost Team Edition
alternatives.desc: Slack-shaped chat below 250 users, self-hosted; the subscription disappears and the pager appears.

alternatives.name: Pumble Free
alternatives.desc: Unlimited users, channels and history with ten gigabytes total; group meetings and serious integrations still cost money.

alternatives.name: Rocket.Chat Community
alternatives.desc: Channels, threads, files and integrations for up to a hundred concurrent users; MongoDB is the hidden teammate.

alternatives.name: Zulip
alternatives.desc: Topic-first team chat with full history and excellent search; fewer drive-by messages survive.

notes: Editorial comparison targets the Pro plan and a single private community DIY substitute. Recheck price before merge.
prompt:
Build a closest honest personal substitute for Slack Pro in an empty repository.
Use Next.js 15, TypeScript, PostgreSQL, Drizzle ORM, WebSockets, and Docker Compose; do not offer alternative stacks.
The core loop is: run a small private team chat with channels, threads, file sharing, and search, and keep membership and moderation under the owner's control.
Make the first run work locally with one documented command.
Store all user data locally by default and make export straightforward.
Put secrets in .env, ship .env.example, and never commit credentials.
Implement spaces, channels, topics, replies, reactions, mentions, profiles, roles, and invitations.
Use WebSockets for live updates but preserve every message transactionally in PostgreSQL.
Add moderation queues, reports, blocks, rate limits, attachment limits, and an audit log.
Provide email digests, browser notifications, search, pinned content, and member export.
Add owner-controlled retention, account deletion, backup, restore, and health checks.
Ship Docker Compose with a seeded demo, migrations, and an emergency admin command.
Include clear empty, loading, success, and recoverable error states.
Add input validation, safe filenames, and graceful handling of unavailable APIs.
Write focused tests for the core transformation and one end-to-end happy path.
Create a README with setup, architecture, permissions, data location, and backup steps.
Do not add accounts, billing, telemetry, analytics, or a hosted control plane.
Do not claim to reproduce proprietary data, network liquidity, regulated access, or frontier infrastructure.
Deliberately leave out public-network discovery and existing member liquidity.
Deliberately leave out production voice or video rooms.
Deliberately leave out native mobile applications, enterprise SSO, and 24-hour abuse operations.
Finish by running the tests and listing the exact commands used.
